story_text.value:
Since the rise of AI coding assistants, about 80% of the dev candidates that I interview tell me that they aren't writing much code themselves anymore - they are directing agents instead. This makes me deeply uncomfortable (although maybe I'm just being old-fashioned). I still want to know that devs on my team can actually write code themselves, and have some idea of what they are doing when it comes to system design. This is increasingly challenging given how rapidly the AI tools are evolving.

I'm curious what other folks are seeing in a post-AI hiring landscape and how you are approaching candidates that tell you they are fully agent-pilled when it comes to their development process. Should I keep doing the conventional leetcode and design interviews? Or just give up and expect everyone is going to use Claude Code no matter what?

title.value: Ask HN: How do you interview devs in a post-AI world?

story_text.value:
Hello folks,

I am a senior Software Engineer working in the IT field for close to 16 years.

Before AI coding tools became prevalent, I enjoyed writing code, architecting software systems, and speaking to the stakeholders. These past 2 - 3 years, since companies have been using AI tools heavily, I noticed most of the work has been delegated to AI. It's just prompting it to do work while I monitor its inputs and outputs, then redefining the prompts.

This work flow really took away my passion and joy of writing and building software systems. I don't know where I am heading next... most of my friends either move on to work on their solopreneur journey or switch careers completely. I can say my passion for building software is definitely diminished due to heavy AI usage

Has anyone experienced this? How do you cope with it? Did you end up switching careers?

thanks for your comments :)

story_text.value: I built AIRUNCODE because I was frustrated by two patterns in current AI coding environments: cloud vendor lock-in that wipes project memory when switching providers, and platforms adding heavy markups on top of user API keys.AIRUNCODE is a local-first desktop runtime (v1.4.7) that executes parallel multi-agent swarms directly against your local workspace. It's fully BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) or compatible with local inference via Ollama/GGUF, so you pay the providers directly with $0 markup.The Architecture:Desktop Shell: Electron 43 with a React 19 / Tailwind 4 interface.Local State & Memory: Powered by SQLite WAL and sqlite-vec to maintain a local, persistent knowledge graph and project index on your machine.Verification Loop: It autodetects local testing frameworks (Vitest, Cargo, pytest, etc.). Agents run tasks in parallel using isolated worktrees and must pass test assertions before completion. If they fail, the system triggers a localized context rollback to protect your main git branch.Graphics Pipeline: For graphics and simulation devs, it features V-CORE Studio, a native runtime built in C++, Vulkan, and SDL3 that allows agents to drive live 3D development and Lua scripting.The packaged binaries are ready for Windows (x64), macOS (Apple Silicon), and Linux.I'm the solo creator and would love to answer any questions about the multi-agent debate coordination, the local context compaction mechanics, or the Vulkan integration. Looking forward to your brutal feedback!

story_text.value:
I spent the last 3 months building my own AI agent harness, fully written in Go. It's called Forcefield, and I primarily built it because I had trouble using local AI models with agent harnesses like Claude Code. I found the configuration needed to get local models working frustrating, and I wanted something simpler.

The main thing I've been optimizing for is the runtime itself. It needs to have low overhead, fast startup, and a simple enough system that users can run it locally without an account or telemetry.

I'd be interested in feedback from people who use local AI coding tools. If you try Forcefield and find any bugs, please open an issue on GitHub. I'm also interested in feedback on the architecture and overall UX.

title.value: Show HN: Forcefield: A fast, lightweight local-first AI agent harness

story_text.value:
ThinkRail is JetBrains' open-source IDE shell for AI coding agents: worktree-per-tab, chat + file tree + terminal, but hardwired to one agent (Pi).

My fork adds a plugin API so it can host others too, starting with Claude Code running in the same UI.

What's new over upstream:

- A prototype of real plugin system - Claude Code as a first-class citizen — config, IDE bridge, and terminal status all wired in as a builtin plugin, so you get Claude Code sessions in the same worktree-scoped UI as `pi`. - Seven other builtin plugins split out the same way: blueprint (interactive specs), PDF preview, branch graph, a live drawing/visualize surface, and file-type icons

Nightly builds via a Homebrew tap are provided.

title.value: Show HN: I forked JetBrains' new agent IDE to host Claude Code

story_text.value:
I spent a while exploring whether AI could help build businesses that operate with little ongoing owner involvement. This was inspired in part by Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench work on AI agents running simulated businesses. Their Project Vend collaboration with Anthropic takes that question into a real shop. (Obviously it was also inspired by "the dream.")

Unfortunately, currently, I think the answer is generally "no." Vending-Bench shows outcomes relative to a well-defined business environment, while starting businesses isn't well-defined and much harder, for us and AI.

But one useful result was this browser simulation, which I'm sharing as a free side project. It basically generalizes the idea behind Vending-Bench itself, but in a simulation that anyone can mess around with, including AI.

Choose a digital product, custom digital service, vending machine, or reusable equipment such as a laundromat. Set demand, costs, staffing and rules, then run 14 simulated days without the owner. Inspect unfinished orders, cash, refunds and requests for your help. Change the setup and rerun the same conditions.

The model supplies fictional customers and failures. AI help has preset outcomes; no model is called by the site. It's a way to explore operating assumptions, not a demand or profit forecast. An optional copy/paste workflow lets your own assistant plan decisions with the fictional fortnight known in advance. It is not thinking live between days.

I developed it with substantial AI coding assistance, automated checks, AI role-playing of users (occupying user types/roles), and feedback from human friends who tried it. It runs in the browser without signup.

Repo here: https://github.com/automatedteach/vending-machine-lab

story_text.value:
I'm the builder of LEO, and this is not a packege or a service.

It's a engineering framework of the rules for Cursor or ClaudeCode, helping to build enorm AI Native projects, 300 000 + lines of code (I understand that is not the quality gate, but - zero TODO, cyclomatic complexity <= 10 (lizard), the project work). A cursorrules file with 44 rules plus 133 *.md files (roles, canons, protocols) that registred how to do an Enterprise project. However, I build solo an AI Nodes Constructor pipeline IDE like n8n for 3-4 month, and if you wont you can look some greps and tests of this project.

368 schema constrants, 77 row-level-security policies, 120+ alembic migrations, 3900+ tests, 10 200+ functions and more.

If you wont to know more about the project and LEO rules: https://dev.to/alex-zaporozhan/385000-lines-of-code-in-three...

Another projects build with LEO (first debute project, open source, enjoy the lines of code): https://github.com/alex-zaporozhan/medCore"

Thank you for your help,

Alex
